entries.title: Where are you taking her
entries.body:
The ant picked up my egg and began walking away with it.

I raised my front legs. Curled my abdomen. Did everything that had worked on the beetles. The ant walked under me.

"Where are you taking her?"

"Down."

"How far down?"

She kept walking. I followed along the branch until there was no branch left. My egg looked very small in her jaws. So did she, suddenly.

I told her to be careful with the little brown one, which was an idiotic thing to say. It was the only one she was carrying.

She disappeared into the ground.

I stayed above the entrance until another ant came out. Asked whether the first had arrived.

"Yes."

I asked if she could tell her thank you.

"Which one?"

I hadn't asked her name.
entries.theme: parental fear and reliance on another species
entries.payoff: Her intimidating display gives way to anxious gratitude toward someone whose name she never asked.

entries.title: Outside lunch
entries.body:
When I was little, everything I touched was edible. It curved around me in every direction. I assumed this was how things were.

Then I chewed a hole through the world.

I pushed my head through. Nothing to bite. Cool air moved over me. I reached farther. Still nothing. There was an unreasonable amount of elsewhere.

I backed in.

I had no legs. No idea what would hold me up outside. All my experience concerned being inside lunch, and I had just given lunch a draft.

I ate a little around the edge of the hole. Made it wider. Tried again.

Eventually I went through.

Now I stand on acorns with six feet and a long face, pretending I have always known about trees.
entries.theme: a limited world opening into a larger life
entries.payoff: An overwhelming first discovery of the outside becomes the adult's concealed history of uncertainty.

entries.title: After you
entries.body:
We tried to kiss goodbye and crossed noses. I backed up. She followed. We tried again.

"You first," she said.

"That's what I'm trying to do."
entries.payoff: Their efforts to be considerate keep colliding.

entries.title: Expansion plans
entries.body:
My leaves went brown one at a time. I kept expecting somebody to say whether I was doing this correctly.

The moss said it happened every year.

That was easy for him to say. He was still green.

I folded into the small tight part of myself and tried to remember what spring felt like. All I could remember was wanting summer. It seemed I had used the whole season waiting for a better one.

"What if I don't wake up?"

The moss considered this.

"I'll grow around you."

I told him I had asked for reassurance, not expansion plans.

He said he would grow around me if I did wake up, too.

I thought about that for a while. Then asked him to leave room for the leaves.
entries.payoff: The moss's apparently alarming answer turns out to include both possible futures.

entries.title: What else is there
entries.body:
Bea told me about the lake. I asked how much water.

She said I wouldn't believe her.

I asked what was past the lake. Trees. Past the trees, more flowers. Past those, she didn't know. She had turned back because it was getting cold.

I had a great many questions about turning back. About choosing a direction. About having the air underneath you instead of above you.

She settled on my flower and said she was tired.

I stopped asking.

After a while I asked whether I was missing much.

"Yes," she said.

I wished she had lied.

Then she put her face into the flower and stayed there so long I wondered if she had fallen asleep.

"You do have this, though," she said.
entries.theme: curiosity, limitation and another creature's pleasure
entries.payoff: Her envy of travel encounters the traveler's pleasure in something she already possesses.

entries.title: Further research
entries.body: Darwin put meat, cheese and bits of glass on my relatives, then wrote a book about what happened. I've read it. I would like to put a few things on Darwin.
entries.theme: the observed organism questions the observer
entries.payoff: The scientific subject proposes reversing the experiment.

references.note: Charles Darwin, Insectivorous Plants,1875, original primary text. Chapters on Drosera include meat, cheese and glass experiments. The narrator's proposed response is invented, not a Darwin quotation.
